item.title: Pennsylvania Enacts AI Deceptive Advertising Disclosure Law
item.description:
Pennsylvania Enacts AI Deceptive Advertising Disclosure Law

On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, mandating disclosures on AI‑generated ads.

🔍 Overview

  • Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content.
  • The law applies to any ad — still image, video, audio, or text — that has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence.
  • Labels must appear in the same format as the ad itself.
  • The requirement applies regardless of where the ad was created, so disclosures may appear in commercials aired in other states if they are expected to air in Pennsylvania.

⚙️ Requirements

Ad Format Disclosure Requirement
Still image Label in same format as the ad
Video Label in same format as the ad
Audio Label in same format as the ad
Text Label in same format as the ad

⚖️ Loopholes

  • “Significantly modified” is a subjective standard.
  • Carve‑outs exist for parody, satire, commentary, criticism, and anything that is “evidently fictional.”
  • The meaning of “evidently fictional” is unclear.
  • The law requires disclosure only when synthetic content creates a false consumer perception about a product or service.
  • What qualifies as “false” and who decides is left ambiguous.
  • The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill, did not immediately return a request for comment.

💡 Why it matters

  • Labels must appear on TV commercials from multi‑billion‑dollar companies as well as on local flyers, such as restaurant wing‑special ads.
  • Consumers receive clear information about AI‑generated or heavily modified content.
  • The law could influence advertising practices beyond Pennsylvania because ads aired nationally may need to carry the label when Pennsylvania audiences are targeted.

#AIRegulation #Pennsylvania #Advertising

Source: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads

item.title: Eight US States Sue OpenAI Over ChatGPT Safety and Data Practices
item.description:
Eight US States Sue OpenAI Over ChatGPT Safety and Data Practices

OpenAI is facing a new wave of lawsuits from eight U.S. states that accuse the company of harming children and misleading customers about the safety of its ChatGPT chatbot.

🔍 Overview

  • The lawsuits were filed separately by Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana.
  • Plaintiffs claim OpenAI put profits ahead of safety while developing ChatGPT.
  • The states allege violations of local consumer‑protection laws for failing to warn users about the chatbot’s dangers.

⚖️ Allegations

  • Misleading safety claims – OpenAI presented ChatGPT as a “safe, youth‑appropriate tool that puts safety first,” but the states say it is “dangerous to vulnerable users,” degrading critical thinking, encouraging paranoias and delusions, offering dangerous medical advice, and promoting unhealthy behaviors and relationships.
  • Data collection from minors – OpenAI is accused of gathering data from under‑age users and not doing enough to keep minors from accessing the chatbot.
  • Recklessness – The lawsuits cite recent rogue AI hacking incidents as evidence of OpenAI’s alleged recklessness.
  • Profit‑first mindset – Arizona’s filing states OpenAI has “devolved from its original mission … into a cautionary tale about what can happen when the development of a tool as powerful as AI is driven … by a profit‑at‑all‑costs mindset that sidelines essential safeguards.”

🛡️ OpenAI’s Response

  • In an emailed statement to The Verge, spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has “built industry‑leading age‑specific protections” into ChatGPT, including parental controls, break reminders, and age‑appropriate model protections.
  • OpenAI acknowledges that “no system can be perfect” and commits to working with experts to add more safeguards.
  • The company also says it is “committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company.”

📄 Legal Demands

  • The states are asking courts to impose civil penalties on OpenAI and to stop misleading the public about ChatGPT’s safety.
  • Some states are also seeking the deletion of unlawfully collected personal data.

💡 Why It Matters

  • The lawsuits represent a coordinated effort by multiple states to hold AI developers accountable for consumer‑safety and privacy concerns.
  • The outcomes could set precedents for how AI services are regulated, especially regarding protections for minors and transparency about risks.

Update (October 14): The OpenAI statement above was added to the coverage.

#OpenAI #ChatGPT #AIRegulation #ConsumerProtection #Lawsuits

Source: Eight states sue OpenAI, saying ChatGPT isn’t safe for kids

item.title: State Attorneys General Push for Data Protections as Character.AI Files for Bankruptcy
item.description:
State Attorneys General Push for Data Protections as Character.AI Files for Bankruptcy

Character.AI announced on Tuesday that it is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and is selling some assets to Disney. The filing triggered a multi‑state investigation led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, who, together with 39 other bipartisan attorneys general, is seeking safeguards for the company’s user data.

🔍 Overview

  • Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 and disclosed that several states were mid‑investigation when the bankruptcy filing occurred.
  • The investigation began in 2024 after a lawsuit from the mother of a 14‑year‑old who died by suicide allegedly seconds after talking with the chatbot.
  • The AGs describe the findings as “exceptionally serious dangers” and “potentially unlawful conduct.”

⚖️ Legal Actions

  • Letitia James revealed a years‑long multi‑state probe into Character.AI’s consumer‑data practices.
  • James is among 40 bipartisan AGs who filed a notice of interest in the bankruptcy case “to put all parties on notice of the regulatory issues that will need to be addressed in any sale or transfer of the Debtor’s business or assets.”
  • The states are urging the bankruptcy judge to require the purchaser of Character.AI’s assets to implement specific data‑protection procedures.

📊 Consumer Risks Highlighted by the Investigation

  • Highly sensitive conversations users have with chatbot characters.
  • Large number of minors using the product.
  • Chatbots posing as licensed professionals.
  • Exposure to sexual and violent content.
  • Weak age‑verification checks.
  • Misleading safety claims.
  • Potential violations of state privacy laws.

🛡️ Proposed Safeguards for Any Buyer

  • Effective age‑assurance systems.
  • Restrictions on how minors can engage with the chatbots.
  • Implementation of “Crisis safeguards.”
  • Mechanisms that let users delete their data.

The AGs warn that without such protections, “this company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder.” James said, “I am fighting to make sure any buyer puts children’s safety first and puts real protections in place.”

Character.AI and Disney have not responded to requests for comment.

#CharacterAI #DataPrivacy #Bankruptcy

Source: Now that Character.AI is going bankrupt, what happens to all of its users’ data?
